vignette:
Sokha is a 31-year-old carpenter who lives with his wife in a small city in the Pacific Northwest. He came to therapy six weeks ago at his wife's insistence. She told him he's not the same person she married-he's distant, quick to anger, and sometimes she finds him sitting alone in the dark at midnight, staring at nothing. He agreed to come, he said, because he's tired of feeling like a ghost in his own life.

The event that fractured his world happened about eighteen months ago. Sokha was driving home from a late-night kitchen renovation, tired and thinking only about a hot shower. He was pulled over for what the officers said was a broken taillight-though the taillight worked fine when they shined their flashlight on it. They ordered him out of the car. Before he could fully stand, one officer grabbed his arm and threw him onto the asphalt. He remembers the gravel scraping his cheek, the weight of a knee on his spine, the tightness of handcuffs that seemed meant to break bone. Words came at him-go back to your country, you think you can just drive around here?-and he could not make them fit into his understanding of his own life. He was a legal citizen, born in a refugee camp, raised here since age four. He had never even gotten a parking ticket. That night he spent in a holding cell, charged with resisting arrest, all charges dropped three weeks later. No apology. No explanation.

After that, Sokha stopped driving at night. He stopped going to the grocery store near the intersection where it happened. He stopped visiting his cousin in the next neighborhood because the route passes a police station. He does not think about these decisions consciously; his body makes them for him. At work, he has become hyper-aware of every car that slows near the job site. When he hears a siren-even from blocks away-his hands freeze on his hammer, and he waits, breath held, until the sound fades. The noise of a table saw sometimes triggers a flashback: the high-pitched whine shortens his vision, and for a second he is on the ground again, the cold concrete against his temple.

He has trouble concentrating on measurements, and twice he has cut a board too short, costing him materials and time. His boss has noticed and asked if something is wrong. Sokha shrugs and says he didn't sleep well. He does not tell anyone what happened. He feels it is his fault-if he had acted submissive, if he had said the right words, maybe the officers would have let him go. The shame sits in his stomach like a stone.

At home his wife tries to touch his shoulder and he flinches. He knows it hurts her but he cannot help it. He lies in bed awake, ears straining for the sound of a car pulling into the driveway, boots on the steps. His sleep is broken by dreams where he is back in that cell, the door slamming shut over and over. He jerks awake gasping, and then lies still, not wanting to wake her. He has started drinking two or three beers every evening just to take the edge off his vigilance.

He avoids crowded places, avoids eye contact with anyone in uniform, avoids talking to his own reflection. The carpentry that once gave him pride-the smell of sawdust, the precision of a dovetail joint-now feels hollow. He goes through the motions because he has bills to pay, but the work no longer gives him meaning. His wife says she misses the man who used to carve her little wooden birds. Those birds sit on a shelf in the living room, untouched. He cannot find his way back to that person. He is here, in this chair, because he does not know what else to do.
